Where it began

Steven Finn was born in Watford on 4 April 1989 and went to Parmiter's School in nearby Garston. He was a good enough basketball player to represent his county, and a loyal follower of Watford Football Club. His cricket began at Langleybury and West Herts.

Middlesex could not wait for him. On 1 June 2005, at 16, he played his first first-class match, against Cambridge UCCE at Fenner's, and took a wicket in each innings. No one had ever played first-class cricket for the county younger, and the record he took had belonged to Fred Titmus since 1949.

The player

England sent for him in a hurry in March 2010, flying him to Bangladesh when their attack was short of bowlers. Days later he was in the Test side, aged 20: England's 647th Test cricketer. That summer he took nine wickets in a match at Lord's and was named Player of the Series against Bangladesh. In the 2010-11 Ashes he took 6 for 125 at the Gabba, and that winter the ICC named him its Emerging Player of the year. In 2011 he became the youngest England bowler to reach 50 Test wickets.

His finest Test came at Edgbaston in 2015, his first for two years. He had Steve Smith out in his first over, then took 6 for 79 in the second innings and was player of the match, and England went on to win the Ashes 3-2. In all he played 36 Tests between 2010 and 2016 and took 125 wickets at 30.40, with five five-wicket innings.

What made him special

He had height, pace and an easy action that he could repeat all day, and he regularly bowled at more than 90 miles an hour. His quickest ball was timed at 151.9 km/h. He was a fine one-day bowler too: in 2015, against Australia, he took a hat-trick, something no England bowler had done at a World Cup before.

Batting was more of a hobby. His 279 Test runs came at 11.16, but he did once make 56, in New Zealand in 2013, and in 2010 he kept Matt Prior company for long enough that Prior reached a hundred.

Away from the middle

He also played for Otago, for Sussex in 2022 and for the Manchester Originals in the first season of The Hundred. In 2019 he joined Test Match Special as a commentator, and he retired from all cricket in August 2023.

And finally

In his early years his knee had a habit of brushing the non-striker's stumps as he bowled, sometimes sending a bail to the ground. In 2013 he changed his run-up, and the game changed its laws to match: a ball that breaks the non-striker's wicket in delivery became a no-ball, a rule known ever since as Finn's Law. Plenty of bowlers have left their mark on the game. Few have done it with a knee.
